newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fiery reformer getting notice in Japan campaign.
newsitem.headline: Fiery reformer getting notice in Japan campaign.

text.p: A fiery political maverick who as Japan's health minister attacked his own agency and then surprised almost everyone by actually making some changes is emerging as a key figure in this election season.

Health Minister Naoto Kan, who has been painted as a hero by the media for his high-profile exposure of an AIDS scandal at his own agency, is expected to parlay his popularity into a key post in Japan's next cabinet.
Kan this weekend helped launch the Democratic Party, brainchild of a group of young politicians striving to create a "third political force" as an alternative to the nation's two conservative camps.

Pundits say the party, expected to appeal to younger, mostly urban voters turned off by old-style politics, could make a substantial showing in elections for the Lower House of parliament on October 20 -- especially now that Kan has joined.
"He's Japan's new hope," said one female office worker.

Bashing bureaucrats for policy mistakes has become standard procedure for politicians here. But Kan has garnered respect among Japan's cynical and apathetic voters for his rare act of following words with action.
A former member of the ruling coalition's tiniest partner, the New Party Sakigake, Kan, 49, was made health and welfare minister when Ryutaro Hashimoto became prime minister last January.

Kan quickly pledged to ferret out ministry files that AIDS activists charged would show bureaucrats were responsible for a 1980s tainted blood scandal that infected some 1,800 haemophiliacs with HIV, the virus that causes AIDS.
To the surprise of many -- perhaps including Hashimoto, who has himself held the health portfolio and has close ties with the pharmaceutical industry -- Kan carried out his promise.
The impact of that move is still reverberating at the ministry and at the drug companies involved.
"I think Hashimoto must have miscalculated," said one Japanese journalist. "He thought he could control Kan."
Kan, the son of an engineer, has spent most of his political career in the opposition wilderness.
An anti-Vietnam War protester at university, he entered politics as a campaign worker for a woman's rights activist.
In 1980, after three failed attempts, Kan won a seat in the Lower House as a member of a small socialist splinter party.
Only after joining Sakigake in 1994, the year the party joined a ruling bloc with the LDP and the Socialists, did Kan glimpse what being on the ruling side could mean.
"He was an opposition-style politician, and his goal was more to be governor of Tokyo than prime minister," said Yasunori Sone, a Keio University political scientist who has known Kan for years.
"But then he had the chance to become a cabinet minister and he realised what power could accomplish."

Associates say Kan, often portrayed as quick to anger, is a pragmatist who works hard to grasp policy issues with the help of a network of private advisers rather than the bureaucratic input on which many politicians rely.
They also credit his wife, Nobuko, with nudging him to take up the AIDS issue and pressing him to battle on when he got discouraged.
Some political analysts say it is not year clear how much Kan's reformist zeal will translate into political clout.

They say that voters seeking change may be sceptical of the new party, having seen their hopes dashed when Morihiro Hosokawa led a reform movement that ousted the long-ruling LDP in 1993 only to step down as prime minister less than a year later.

Still, many say popular dissatisfaction and the impact of a new electoral system giving urban votes greater weight could help the Democrats win enough seats to secure a place in a new ruling coalition and another cabinet portfolio for Kan.
